title: TCP U2·W2 — Entity Tax Planning Deep-Dive (2026)
lessonHtml:
Cold open — the life cycle of an entity's tax

Entity choice (Unit 1) is only the start; operating a pass-through or corporation tax-efficiently requires planning at every stage — formation, distributions, conversions, and liquidation. Each is governed by precise rules with large planning consequences for MBG and its owner. This week works the deep entity mechanics on the 2026 Public Law 119-21 baseline: tax-free formation, the dividend-versus-sale character of distributions, the S-corporation built-in gains trap, partnership allocations and the §754 election, and the tax of winding down.

Tax-free formation

Contributing property to a new entity is generally tax-free. Under §351, transferors who contribute property to a corporation and control at least 80% of it afterward recognize no gain, taking a substituted basis in their stock (gain is recognized only to the extent of boot received). Under §721, contributing property to a partnership is tax-free with no control requirement, and the partner's outside basis includes the contributed basis plus a share of partnership debt. Planning watch-outs: contributing property subject to debt exceeding basis can trigger gain, and contributing services (not property) is taxable compensation.

Corporate distributions — dividend versus return of capital

A corporate distribution is a dividend to the extent of earnings and profits (E&P), taxable at qualified-dividend rates; beyond E&P it is a tax-free return of capital (reducing stock basis), then capital gain. The planning question is often whether to bleed earnings out as salary (deductible to a C corp, ordinary to the owner) or dividends (non-deductible, double-taxed) — and whether to retain earnings to defer the second tax (watching the accumulated earnings and personal holding company penalty taxes). For a closely held corporation, balancing reasonable salary against distributions is the central recurring decision.

Stock redemptions

A redemption (the corporation buying back a shareholder's stock) is taxed as a sale (capital gain, basis recovered) only if it is sufficiently disproportionate under §302 — a complete termination of interest, a substantially disproportionate redemption (the shareholder drops below 80% of their prior ownership and below 50% control), or one "not essentially equivalent to a dividend." Otherwise the entire amount is a dividend (no basis recovery). The family attribution rules complicate this in closely held firms — a parent is treated as owning a child's shares — so a redemption intended as a clean sale can be recharacterized as a dividend without careful structuring (or a waiver of attribution).

The S-corporation built-in gains tax

A C corporation that converts to an S corporation faces the built-in gains (BIG) tax (§1374) — a corporate-level tax on gains that were built in at the conversion date if the asset is sold within the recognition period. The BIG tax exists to stop firms from using an S election to escape the C-corporation double tax on appreciation that accrued while a C corp. Planning around it means holding appreciated assets past the recognition period or timing dispositions, and tracking the net unrealized built-in gain. S-corporation distributions are also ordered against the accumulated adjustments account (AAA), generally tax-free to the extent of basis — another account a planner monitors.

Partnership distributions and hot assets

Partnership distributions are usually tax-free under §731 — a partner recognizes gain only when cash distributed exceeds outside basis, and takes a basis in distributed property. The major exception is §751 "hot assets" — unrealized receivables and substantially appreciated inventory — which carry ordinary-income character that cannot be converted to capital gain through a distribution or sale of the partnership interest. A planner distinguishes current from liquidating distributions and tracks hot assets, because they are where a seemingly tax-free partnership transaction generates ordinary income.

Special allocations and the §754 election

Partnerships offer flexibility corporations cannot. Special allocations let partners divide specific items disproportionately to ownership if they have substantial economic effect (reflected in capital accounts and liquidation). The §754 election lets the partnership adjust the basis of its assets when an interest is sold (§743(b)) or property is distributed (§734(b)), so an incoming partner's inside basis matches what they paid — preventing a buyer from being taxed on the seller's built-in gain. The §754 election is a powerful but permanent planning choice that a sophisticated partnership uses to keep inside and outside basis aligned.

Liquidations

Winding down has its own tax. A corporate liquidation is generally taxed twice: the corporation recognizes gain as if it sold its assets at fair value (§336), and shareholders recognize gain on the difference between the distribution and their stock basis (§331) — a major cost that argues against the C-corp form for assets expected to appreciate. A partnership liquidation is generally tax-free under §731 except for cash exceeding basis and hot assets. Anticipating the exit tax at formation is the integrative lesson: the entity chosen on day one determines the tax on the day the business is sold or wound down.

Reorganizations and tax-free combinations

Beyond formation and liquidation, the Code permits tax-free reorganizations — mergers and acquisitions structured to defer gain. A qualifying statutory merger (Type A), stock-for-stock (Type B), or stock-for-assets (Type C) reorganization lets shareholders exchange their stock for acquirer stock without recognizing gain (except to the extent of boot), carrying over basis and the target's tax attributes. The planning trade-off mirrors a sale: a taxable acquisition gives the buyer a stepped-up basis (future depreciation) but triggers the seller's gain now, while a tax-free reorganization defers the seller's tax but leaves the buyer with carryover basis. The continuity-of-interest and continuity-of-business-enterprise doctrines, plus a valid business purpose, are the requirements that keep a reorganization tax-free, and net operating losses and other attributes carry to the acquirer but are limited by §382 when ownership changes — a key diligence item in any deal. Structuring a combination to balance the buyer's and seller's tax positions is sophisticated entity planning a CPA supports.

CMA bridge

For MBG, the entity life cycle is the CFO's tax map: structuring a tax-free §351/§721 contribution at formation, setting Jordan Reed's salary-versus-distribution mix, using a §754 election if ownership changes, and anticipating the double tax on a C-corp liquidation. Planning the exit at formation — not at sale — is what captures the value TCP teaches.

Practice and recap

  1. Form tax-free: §351 (corp, 80% control, boot triggers gain) / §721 (partnership, no control test, basis includes debt); services are taxable.
  2. Tax distributions: dividend to extent of E&P, then return of capital, then gain; redemptions are a sale only if they meet §302 (watch family attribution).
  3. Plan the S-corp built-in gains tax (§1374 recognition period) and AAA-ordered distributions; handle §751 hot assets in partnership distributions.
  4. Use special allocations (substantial economic effect) and the §754 election (§743/§734 basis adjustments); anticipate the double tax on corporate liquidation (§331/§336).

Recap: entity tax planning spans the life cycle — §351/§721 make formation tax-free (boot or excess debt triggers gain); distributions are dividends to the extent of E&P then return of capital, and redemptions are sales only under §302 (family attribution complicates closely held firms); the S-corporation built-in gains tax and AAA ordering, plus §751 hot assets in partnerships, are the traps; special allocations and the §754 election give partnerships basis flexibility; and corporate liquidation's double tax (§331/§336) makes anticipating the exit at formation the integrative discipline.

flashcards.back: §351 (corporation): tax-free if transferors of property control ≥80% after; gain only to extent of boot; substituted basis. §721 (partnership): tax-free, NO control test; outside basis includes share of debt. Services = taxable.
Dividend to the extent of E&P (taxable) → return of capital (tax-free, reduces basis) → capital gain. Watch accumulated-earnings and PHC penalty taxes on excess retention.

Taxed as a SALE (capital gain, basis recovered) only if disproportionate: complete termination, substantially disproportionate (<80% of prior + <50% control), or not essentially equivalent to a dividend. Else = dividend. Family attribution applies.
Corporate-level tax when a former C corp (now S corp) sells assets with built-in gain within the recognition period. Plan: hold appreciated assets past the period; track net unrealized built-in gain.
Unrealized receivables + substantially appreciated inventory carry ORDINARY-income character that can't be converted to capital gain via a distribution or sale of the partnership interest.

Lets a partnership adjust asset (inside) basis on a sale of an interest (§743(b)) or a distribution (§734(b)) so inside basis matches outside — protects a buyer from the seller's built-in gain. Permanent election.
Partners may divide specific items disproportionately to ownership IF the allocation has substantial economic effect (reflected in capital accounts and liquidation).
Corporate: double tax — corp gain as if assets sold at FMV (§336) + shareholder gain (§331). Partnership: generally tax-free (§731) except cash > basis and hot assets. Plan the exit at formation.

questions.q: A §351 tax-free incorporation requires the property transferors to control, immediately after:
questions.explain: §351 nonrecognition requires the transferors of property to control ≥80% of the corporation afterward.

questions.q: A corporate distribution is a taxable dividend to the extent of:
questions.explain: Distributions are dividends to the extent of E&P, then a return of capital, then gain.

questions.q: A stock redemption is taxed as a sale (not a dividend) when it:
questions.explain: Only redemptions qualifying under §302 (disproportionate, complete termination, etc.) get sale treatment.

questions.q: The built-in gains tax applies to:
choices: A former C corporation (now S corp) selling appreciated assets within the recognition period
questions.explain: §1374 taxes gains built in at the C-to-S conversion if recognized during the recognition period.

questions.q: Partnership '§751 hot assets' (receivables, appreciated inventory) carry:
choices: Ordinary-income character that can't be converted to capital gain
questions.explain: Hot assets preserve ordinary income even on a sale or distribution of the partnership interest.

questions.q: A §754 election allows a partnership to:
choices: Adjust inside asset basis on a transfer or distribution to match outside basis
questions.explain: §754 enables §743(b)/§734(b) basis adjustments so inside basis aligns with what a buyer paid.

questions.q: A complete liquidation of a C corporation generally results in:
choices: Tax at both the corporate and shareholder levels
questions.explain: The corporation recognizes gain (§336) and shareholders recognize gain (§331) — double tax.
